subject: Economy
sub_topic: Five Year Plans — legacy and approach

concepts.name: Planning Commission: Constitutional Status, Composition, and Mandate
key_dimensions: Extra-constitutional body established by executive resolution (1950) — no statutory or constitutional backing
PM as ex-officio Chairman; distinction from Finance Commission (constitutional body) — common UPSC trap
Mandate: assessment of resources, formulation of plans for effective utilisation, advisory vs. allocative role
Abolition in 2014 and replacement by NITI Aayog — continuity vs. rupture debate

concepts.name: Harrod-Domar Growth Model and its Application in Early Five Year Plans
key_dimensions: Core logic: growth rate = savings rate ÷ capital-output ratio; implications for high investment strategy
Rationale for adopting this model in 1st and 2nd Plans — capital scarcity in post-colonial India
Criticism: ignores technological change, human capital, and structural rigidities in Indian economy
Contrast with later shift toward Solow-type and multisector models in subsequent plans

concepts.name: First Five Year Plan (1951–56): Priorities, Model, and Outcomes
key_dimensions: Based on Harrod-Domar model; primary focus on agriculture, irrigation, and rehabilitation of refugees
Only plan where actual growth exceeded target (3.6% vs. 2.1% target) — frequently tested fact
Role of community development programme (1952) and National Extension Service
Contrast with Second Plan's shift away from agriculture — sets up the Mahalanobis debate

concepts.name: Mahalanobis Model and the Second Five Year Plan (1956–61)
key_dimensions: Two-sector model: emphasis on heavy industry and capital goods to build long-run productive capacity
Theoretical basis: expanding capital goods sector generates future consumption goods autonomously
Nehru-Mahalanobis strategy: socialist pattern of society, public sector dominance, import substitution
Criticisms — neglect of agriculture, employment generation, and foreign exchange crisis of late 1950s

concepts.name: Industrial Policy Resolution 1956 and its Link to Planning Framework
key_dimensions: Classified industries into three schedules: exclusive public sector, mixed, and private sector
Operationalised 'socialist pattern of society' goal from Second Plan period
Instrument of dirigisme: licensing raj, MRTP Act linkage, and restrictions on private capital
UPSC trap: IPR 1948 vs. IPR 1956 — differences in scope and ideological grounding

concepts.name: Plan Holiday (1966–69): Causes, Implications, and Annual Plans
key_dimensions: Causes: Indo-Pak war (1965), drought (1965–66), devaluation of rupee (1966), foreign aid suspension
Three annual plans substituted for Fourth Five Year Plan — significance for continuity of planning
Green Revolution launched during this period outside formal plan framework — decoupling of policy and planning
Debate: did plan holiday expose structural weaknesses of central planning model?

concepts.name: Gadgil Formula and Centre-State Plan Fund Allocation
key_dimensions: Introduced in Third Plan; formalised in 1969 for allocation of central assistance to state plans
Criteria: population (60%), per capita income (10%), tax effort, ongoing projects, special problems
Revised Gadgil-Mukherjee Formula (1990) — changes in weightage, inclusion of special category states
UPSC trap: Gadgil Formula vs. Finance Commission devolution — different streams, different criteria

concepts.name: Fourth and Fifth Plan Period: Garibi Hatao, Poverty Targeting, and MNP/IRDP
key_dimensions: Shift from growth-only to growth-with-redistribution paradigm — political economy context
Minimum Needs Programme (MNP) in Fifth Plan: basic services approach for rural poor
IRDP (Integrated Rural Development Programme) — asset transfer model, later evaluated as leaky
Fifth Plan terminated one year early (1978) by Janata government — political interruption of planning

concepts.name: Rolling Plan Concept: Janata Government Experiment (1978–80)
key_dimensions: Concept: annual revision of targets and resources to reflect ground realities — Gunnar Myrdal's influence
Replaces rigid five-year targets with three overlapping plans: current year, perspective, and rolling
Criticism: loss of long-term perspective, difficulty in accountability, abandoned by returning Congress govt
UPSC trap: Rolling plan ≠ Annual Plan; distinguish from plan holidays

concepts.name: Sixth Five Year Plan (1980–85): Poverty Alleviation Architecture and Structural Shift
key_dimensions: First plan to explicitly integrate poverty alleviation as central objective alongside growth
Introduced IRDP, NREP, TRYSEM — disaggregated targeting of rural poor, women, tribals
Shift from trickle-down hypothesis to direct intervention model
Beginning of indicative planning debate: private sector given larger role than in earlier plans

concepts.name: Seventh Five Year Plan (1985–90): Infrastructure, Food Security, and Productivity Focus
key_dimensions: Emphasis on 'food, work, and productivity' — Rajiv Gandhi modernisation agenda
Technology Mission approach: targeted programmes for specific sectors (oilseeds, literacy, etc.)
Highest growth rate achieved in any plan up to that point (~6%)
Transition toward market-friendly reforms — sets stage for 1991 liberalisation

concepts.name: 1991 Economic Crisis and its Impact on Planning Approach: Shift to Indicative Planning
key_dimensions: BoP crisis forced structural adjustment — IMF conditionality incompatible with command planning
Eighth Plan (1992–97): explicit shift to indicative planning, market mechanisms, private investment
Delicensing, disinvestment, and trade liberalisation altered the resource mobilisation assumptions of planning
UPSC trap: 'indicative planning' defined — state sets targets but does not direct private sector allocation

concepts.name: Eighth Five Year Plan (1992–97): Human Development Orientation
key_dimensions: Influenced by UNDP Human Development Reports — HDI framework enters Indian planning vocabulary
Focus on human capital: education, health, population control as core plan objectives
Narasimha Rao government: first plan under liberalisation regime — reconciling plan with market
Decentralisation thrust: 73rd/74th Amendments (1992) mandated PRIs as planning units at grassroots

concepts.name: 73rd/74th Constitutional Amendments and Decentralised Planning
key_dimensions: Article 243G: devolution of planning functions to Panchayats — Schedule 11 has 29 subjects
District Planning Committees (Article 243ZD) to consolidate rural and urban plans
Gap between constitutional mandate and actual fiscal/functional devolution — implementation failure
UPSC trap: DPC is constitutional but not uniformly constituted; Metropolitan Planning Committee (Art. 243ZE) often neglected

concepts.name: Tenth Five Year Plan (2002–07): Monitorable Targets and Governance Focus
key_dimensions: First plan to set explicit, time-bound monitorable targets for 11 indicators (poverty, literacy, IMR, etc.)
Introduced concept of state development reports and differential plan strategies for states
Bharat Nirman not a plan but a complement — distinguish from plan flagship schemes
Shift from input-based to outcome-based accountability — precursor to results framework

concepts.name: Eleventh Five Year Plan (2007–12): Inclusive Growth Framework
key_dimensions: 'Faster and More Inclusive Growth' — 9% growth target with equity and sustainability riders
Introduced 27 monitorable targets across income, education, health, women, infrastructure, environment
JNNURM, NRHM, MGNREGS as flagship schemes embedded in plan philosophy
Debate: actual growth ~8% but inclusivity outcomes mixed — jobless growth critique

concepts.name: Twelfth Five Year Plan (2012–17): Faster, Sustainable, and More Inclusive Growth
key_dimensions: Growth target revised down to 8% from 9% — recognition of global slowdown and infrastructure constraints
Three-pillar framework: faster growth + sustainability (environment) + inclusivity
Last Five Year Plan before dissolution of Planning Commission — UPSC frequently asks terminal date
Introduced 'green accounting' and natural capital concepts into mainstream planning discourse

concepts.name: NITI Aayog vs. Planning Commission: Structural and Functional Differences
key_dimensions: NITI Aayog (Jan 2015): think tank model, no fund allocation power — unlike Planning Commission
Cooperative federalism rhetoric: states as 'partners' not recipients; PM chairs, CMs on Governing Council
Instruments: Strategy for New India @75, Vision 2035, SDG India Index — advisory not allocative
UPSC trap: NITI Aayog cannot allocate plan funds; that role shifted to Finance Ministry/Finance Commission

concepts.name: Perspective Planning vs. Five Year Plan vs. Annual Plan: Hierarchy and Instruments
key_dimensions: Perspective plan: 15–20 year long-term vision (e.g., India Vision 2020, Perspective Plan 1961–76)
Five Year Plan: medium-term operational plan with resource allocation and sectoral targets
Annual Plan: one-year rolling slice of Five Year Plan; also used during plan holidays
UPSC trap: Annual Plan ≠ Union Budget; Annual Plan is the planning document, budget is the fiscal instrument

concepts.name: Plan Expenditure vs. Non-Plan Expenditure: Distinction, Criticism, and Abolition
key_dimensions: Plan expenditure: new capital creation linked to plan objectives; Non-plan: maintenance, salaries, interest
Criticism: artificial distinction led to neglect of O&M of created assets — Rangarajan Committee findings
Abolished from Union Budget 2017–18 — replaced by capital and revenue expenditure classification
UPSC trap: abolition of plan/non-plan ≠ abolition of planning; conflation is a common error
